This is a listing of the highest-grossing films by year, based on their United States box-office gross. The films are listed by in-year release, rather than the gross they accumulated during a calendar year.[1]

<fragment>

Six different directors have directed the highest-grossing film on multiple occasions: George Lucas, Steven Spielberg, James Cameron, Sam Raimi, Robert Zemeckis, and Chris Columbus. Spielberg has the record, directing four of the yearly highest-grossing films: *Raiders of the Lost Ark* (1981), *E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial* (1982), *Jurassic Park* (1993), and *Saving Private Ryan* (1998). Lucas has directed three such films, all of which are part of the *Star Wars* franchise, which he created: the original *Star Wars* (1977), and two of its prequels *The Phantom Menace* (1999), and *Revenge of the Sith* (2005). James Cameron has also directed three such films: *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* (1991), *Titanic* (1997), and *Avatar* (2009). Sam Raimi, Robert Zemeckis and Chris Columbus have directed two each: *Spider-Man* (2002) and *Spider-Man 3* (2007) for Raimi; *Back to the Future* (1985) and *Forrest Gump* (1994) for Zemeckis; *Home Alone* (1990) and *Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone* (2001) for Columbus.

In 2008, Emmerich directed *10,000 BC*, a film about the journeys of a prehistoric tribe of mammoth hunters. It was a box office hit, but consistently regarded by professional critics as his worst film, as well as one of the worst films of the year.[22] He was slated to direct a remake of the 1966 science-fiction film *Fantastic Voyage*,[23] but the project slipped back into development hell. In 2009, Emmerich directed *2012*,[24] an apocalyptic disaster film based on the conspiracy theory that the ancient Mayans prophesied the world's ending on 21 December 2012.[25] Despite mixed reviews, the film went on to be his second-highest-grossing film to date (after *Independence Day*) and received praise from audiences. Emmerich usually finishes production of a large-scale movie both in a time frame shorter and on a budget lower than what is typically requested by other directors.[6][8]



### 2010s

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

His next film, *Godzilla*, opened in 1998. An extensive advertising and marketing campaign generated significant hype during the months leading up to the film's release. The film was a box office success but was met with negative reviews from critics and fans. It garnered a Saturn Award for Best Special Effects, a BMI Film Music Award, and the Audience Award for Best Director at the European Film Awards while also receiving a Razzie Award for Worst Remake or Sequel. It has only a 16% rating on Rotten Tomatoes.[18] Emmerich said that prior to getting involved with *Godzilla* he and Devlin had planned a disaster movie centered around an asteroid fall, which wound up cancelled after *Armageddon* went for a similar idea.[1]

<document>
<title>Armageddon (1998 film)</title>
<fragment>

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

<fragment>
Despite a mixed critical reception, a DVD edition of *Armageddon* was released by The Criterion Collection, a specialist film distributor of primarily arthouse films that markets what it considers to be "important classic and contemporary films" and "cinema at its finest". In an essay supporting the selection of *Armageddon*, film scholar Jeanine Basinger, who taught Michael Bay at Wesleyan University, states that the film is "a work of art by a cutting-edge artist who is a master of movement, light, color, and shape—and also of chaos, razzle-dazzle, and explosion". She sees it as a celebration of working men: "This film makes these ordinary men noble, lifting their efforts up into an epic event." Further, she states that in the first few moments of the film all the main characters are well established, saying, "If that isn't screenwriting, I don't know what is".[16]


</fragment>
<fragment>
*Armageddon* received mostly mixed reviews from film critics, many of whom took issue with "the furious pace of its editing".[27] On the review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, the film has a 43% "Rotten" approval rating based on 176 reviews, with an average rating of 5.3/10. The critical consensus states, "Lovely to look at but about as intelligent as the asteroid that serves as the movie's antagonist, *Armageddon* slickly sums up the cinematic legacies of producer Jerry Bruckheimer and director Michael Bay."[28] Metacritic gave the film a weighted average score of 42 out of 100, based on 23 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews". Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film an average grade of "A−" on an A+ to F scale.[29]

The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

[edit]

Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

## **Armageddon (1998) - Complete Plot Synopsis**

### **Asteroid Discovery**
The film begins with the catastrophic Shoemaker-Levy 9 comet impact on Jupiter as a historical precedent. In the present day, NASA discovers a massive asteroid, approximately the size of Texas, composed primarily of iron, on a direct collision course with Earth. The asteroid is detected after it destroys a small space shuttle carrying thousands of spiders for an experiment, leading to widespread panic when debris starts raining down on Earth, including spectacular meteor showers.

### **NASA's Desperate Plan**
After initial attempts to destroy the asteroid with conventional weapons fail, NASA executive Dan Truman (Billy Bob Thornton) realizes they need an unconventional solution. The best option is to drill deep into the asteroid's core and detonate a nuclear warhead to split it apart before it reaches Earth. However, NASA's own drilling equipment isn't sophisticated enough, and they only have 18 days before impact.

### **Recruitment of Oil Drillers**
Truman approaches Harry Stamper (Bruce Willis), the world's foremost deep-core driller, who operates an oil rig in the South China Sea. Harry is initially reluctant but agrees to help after Truman threatens to imprison his crew and reveals the global stakes. Harry insists on bringing his own team of roughneck oil drillers, including:

- **A.J. Frost** (Ben Affleck) - Harry's best driller and boyfriend of his daughter Grace
- **Bear** (Michael Clarke Duncan) - Gentle giant with a big heart
- **Rockhound** (Steve Buscemi) - Womanizing geologist
- **Oscar** (Owen Wilson) - Cocky driller with nerves of steel
- **Lev Andropov** (Peter Stormare) - Russian cosmonaut
- **Charles "Chick" Chapple** (Will Patton) - Veteran driller trying to reconnect with his family
- **Max** (Ken Hudson Campbell) - Overweight driller
- **Watts** (Robert Burgh) - Youngest member of the team

### **Training and Preparation**
The drillers undergo intense, often chaotic NASA astronaut training at Johnson Space Center. The training sequence showcases their lack of military discipline and their blue-collar approach to problem-solving. Key moments include:

- Physical conditioning and equipment familiarization
- Grueling spacewalk simulations
- Learning to operate space shuttles and equipment
- Comic relief as they struggle with NASA protocols
- A.J. and Harry's relationship is strained due to Harry's protective nature toward Grace

### **Space Mission Launch**
Two space shuttles, **Freedom** and **Independence**, launch successfully carrying the drilling crews and nuclear warheads. The launch sequence is dramatic, showing the magnitude of their mission as they leave Earth behind. During their journey through space:

- The mission begins with 12 days remaining
- The crew experiences various technical challenges
- Personal relationships develop further, particularly between A.J. and Harry

### **Tragic Events and Setbacks**
A major catastrophe occurs when the Independence shuttle is destroyed by asteroid debris, killing most of its crew, including Oscar and Max. Only Lev Andropov and Bear survive. The remaining crew on Freedom must adapt to this loss and continue the mission with fewer resources.

The Freedom shuttle makes a harrowing landing on the asteroid's surface, but they overshoot their intended landing zone and end up in a volatile, metallic area that makes drilling extremely difficult.

### **Drilling Operation on the Asteroid**
The drilling operation faces multiple setbacks:

- The asteroid surface is iron, much harder than rock, making drilling extremely difficult
- Equipment failures and malfunctions plague their efforts
- A gas pocket explosion kills one crew member
- The drill constantly breaks due to the extreme conditions
- Communication with Earth becomes unstable

### **The Untimely Arrival**
Just as the team begins making progress with the drilling, military commanders on Earth decide to execute their backup plan - detonating the nuclear weapon remotely, which would risk failing to split the asteroid properly. Harry must persuade them to wait while his team completes the drilling.

### **Sacrifice and Resolution**
When the drilling develops a critical problem with the warhead's detonator unable to be armed remotely, Harry realizes someone must manually stay behind to trigger it while the others escape. In a climactic moment:

- Harry volunteers for the suicide mission
- He performs a last-minute "marriage" ceremony for A.J. and Grace via video communication
- A emotional farewell between father and daughter
- Harry successfully detonates the warhead, sacrificing himself to save Earth

### **Earth's Salvation**
The asteroid splits into two large pieces that safely pass by Earth, preventing global extinction. The remaining crew members return to Earth as heroes, greeted with global celebration. The film ends with Grace mourning her father's sacrifice while embracing A.J., who now carries on Harry's legacy as a responsible husband and father figure.

### **Epilogue**
The final scenes show the characters rebuilding their lives:

- A.J. and Grace marry and have a child, with photos of Harry prominently displayed
- The surviving crew members return to their oil drilling careers, forever changed by their experience
- Humanity is saved but at great personal cost

This plot covers all major story elements: the scientific discovery of the asteroid, the recruitment of unconventional heroes, their challenging training, the dangerous space mission, the drilling operations on the asteroid, and ultimately how Harry's sacrifice saves Earth from imminent destruction.

## Complete Plot Summary of Armageddon (1998)

### Asteroid Discovery
The film begins with NASA discovering a massive asteroid the size of Texas hurtling through space on a direct collision course with Earth. Upon calculating its trajectory, they determine it will impact Earth in just 18 days, leading to total extinction of all life. NASA director Dan Truman realizes that conventional nuclear weapons detonated on the surface would be ineffective due to the asteroid's composition.

### Recruitment of Oil Drillers
Dr. Truman contacts Harry Stamper, a deep-core oil driller and weapons expert, who suggests the only way to stop the asteroid is to drill deep into its core and detonate a nuclear weapon from within. However, NASA's astronauts lack the drilling expertise needed for such a complex operation. Harry agrees to lead the mission on one condition: he can bring his own team of roughneck oil drillers. His crew includes A.J. Frost (who's secretly dating Harry's daughter Grace), Rockhound, Chick, Bear, Max, and Oscar.

### Training
The oil drillers are taken to NASA for astronaut training. They struggle with the rigors of space training - dealing with zero gravity simulators, physical conditioning, and learning spacecraft operations. During this period, tensions arise between Harry and A.J. over A.J.'s relationship with Grace, and the drillers clash with the military mindset of NASA personnel. The team eventually adapts and becomes somewhat space-worthy.

### Space Mission
Two space shuttles, Freedom and Independence, launch to carry the team to the asteroid. The journey is challenging, with the team facing various technical difficulties and personal conflicts. Both shuttles successfully land on the asteroid, though Independence is badly damaged during landing and crashes.

### Events on the Asteroid
The drilling operation proves more difficult than anticipated due to the asteroid's unexpected iron-hard composition. They struggle to reach the required depth before the asteroid reaches zero barrier (the point where it can no longer be diverted). During the drilling, they face numerous crises including equipment failures, unexpected geological formations, and injuries among the crew member.

Additionally, the team must deal with smaller asteroid fragments and debris that continue to endanger their mission. Several crew members are killed during the operation, including Max when he's blown out into space and GRAB (a remote-controlled drill) when it detonates prematurely.

### How They Save Earth
As time runs out, President Truman orders the military to detonate the nuclear weapon remotely from Earth, which would destroy the asteroid but not divert it. Harry realizes they must sacrifice one person to stay behind and manually detonate the bomb at the perfect moment to split the asteroid in two. 

In the emotional climax, A.J. is chosen to return to Earth, but Harry switches places with him, insisting on staying behind. Before staying, Harry gives his blessing to A.J. and Grace's relationship through a video message. Harry successfully detonates the nuclear weapon, splitting the asteroid into two pieces that pass safely by Earth, saving humanity.

The mission succeeds at tremendous personal cost, but Earth is saved. The surviving crew members return as heroes, with A.J. and Grace finally able to be together, and Harry remembered as a martyr who sacrificed himself to save the world.

This covers the complete storyline including the asteroid discovery, recruitment and training of the oil drillers, the space mission, events on the asteroid, and the ultimate sacrifice that saves Earth.

<document>
<title>Deep Impact (film)</title>
<fragment>

*Deep Impact* was released in the same summer as the similarly themed *Armageddon*, which fared better at the box office, while astronomers described *Deep Impact* as being more scientifically accurate.[4][5] Both films were similarly received by critics, with *Armageddon* scoring 43% and *Deep Impact* scoring 45% on Rotten Tomatoes. *Deep Impact* grossed over $349.5 million worldwide on an $80 million production budget. It was the final film by cinematographer Dietrich Lohmann, who died before the film's release.[6]




## Plot

[edit]

In May 1998, at a star party in Virginia, teenage amateur astronomer Leo Biederman observes an unidentified object in the night sky. He sends a picture to astronomer Dr. Marcus Wolf, who realizes it is a comet on collision course with Earth. Wolf dies in a car crash while racing to raise the alarm.


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Deep Impact". *The Numbers*. Nash Information Services. Archived from the original on February 14, 2013. Retrieved February 1, 2013.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Deep Impact". *Box Office Mojo*. Archived from the original on January 1, 2013. Retrieved February 1, 2013.
3. **^** Stweart, Bhob. "Deep Impact". *Allmovie*. RhythmOne. Archived from the original on December 19, 2013. Retrieved August 12, 2012.
4. **^** "Disaster Movies". *Box Office Mojo*. Archived from the original on June 12, 2004. Retrieved March 23, 2008.
5. **^** Plait, Phil (February 17, 2000). "Hollywood Does the Universe Wrong". *Space.com*. TechMedia Network. Archived from the original on October 12, 2010.
6. **^** Oliver, Myrna (November 20, 1997). "Dietrich Lohmann; Widely Praised Cinematographer". *Los Angeles Times*. Archived from the original on March 6, 2016. Retrieved August 18, 2015.

</fragment>
<fragment>
The origins of *Deep Impact* started in the late 1970s when producers Richard Zanuck and David Brown approached Paramount Pictures proposing a remake of the 1951 film *When Worlds Collide*.[7] Although several screenplay drafts were completed, the producers were not completely happy with any of them and the project remained in "development hell" for many years. In the mid-1990s, they approached director Steven Spielberg, with whom they had made the 1975 blockbuster *Jaws*, to discuss their long-planned project.[7] However, Spielberg had already bought the film rights to the 1993 novel *The Hammer of God* by Arthur C. Clarke, which dealt with a similar theme of an asteroid on a collision course for Earth and humanity's attempts to prevent its own extinction. Spielberg planned to produce and direct *The Hammer of God* himself for his then-fledgling DreamWorks studio, but opted to merge the two projects with Zanuck and Brown, and they commissioned a screenplay for what would become *Deep Impact*.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>
7. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** Shapiro, Mark (May 1998). "When Worlds Collide Anew (On Location for Deep Impact...)". *Starlog*. New York, US: Starlog Group, Inc. Retrieved July 15, 2017.
8. **^** "Deep Impact". *The Film Journal*. **98** (1–6). Pubsun Corporation. 1995. Archived from the original on February 24, 2021. Retrieved July 14, 2017.
9. **^** "Arthur C's Pool Of Knowledge". *Saga Magazine*. Saga plc. 1997. Archived from the original on August 10, 2017. Retrieved July 14, 2017.
10. **^** "Deep Impact - Full Cast and Credits - 1998". *Hollywood.com*. Archived from the original on August 10, 2017. Retrieved June 25, 2018.
11. **^** *TV Guide Film and Video Companion 2005*. Barnes & Noble. 2004. p. 232. ISBN 978-0760761045.
12. **^** Grant, Edmund (1999). *The Motion Picture Guide 1999 Annual*. Cinebooks. p. 94. ISBN 978-0933997431.

</fragment>
</document>

<title>Armageddon (1998 film)</title>
<fragment>

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

<document>
<title>Armageddon (1998 film)</title>
<fragment>

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.




## Plot

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

![](image)Bay (left) and Jerry Bruckheimer during the filming of 1998's *Armageddon*
In 1998, Bay again collaborated with Jerry Bruckheimer, this time as a co-producer, as well as directing the action-adventure film *Armageddon*.[31][32] The film, about a group of tough oil drillers who are sent by NASA to deflect an asteroid from a collision course with Earth, starred Bruce Willis, Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck and Liv Tyler. It was nominated for four Oscars at the 71st Academy Awards, including Best Sound, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound Editing and Best Original Song.[33] It earned $9.6 million on its opening day and $36.5 million through the first weekend.[34] Its budget of $140 million was one of the highest of the summer of 1998. It went on to gross over $553 million worldwide, the highest-grossing film of that year.[35]

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.




## Plot

[edit]

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

Based on the 1998 asteroid disaster film, here's the plot synopsis:

**Overview**
The story begins when NASA discovers a massive asteroid the size of Texas hurtling toward Earth on a collision course that will destroy all life on the planet within 18 days. With conventional methods like nuclear weapons deemed ineffective for destroying the asteroid, NASA develops a desperate plan to send a team to drill into the asteroid's core and detonate a nuclear bomb from within to split it apart.

**Recruiting the Team**
Realizing they need the world's best deep-core drillers for this impossible mission, NASA recruits Harry Stamper (played by Bruce Willis) and his rough-and-tumble oil rig crew. Stamper and his men - including A.J. Frost (Ben Affleck), who is in a relationship with Harry's daughter Grace (Liv Tyler), and various colorful characters like Rockhound (Steve Buscemi) and Bear (Michael Clarke Duncan) - are initially reluctant but ultimately agree to save their families and the world.

**Training and Preparation**
The oil drillers undergo intense astronaut training at NASA, struggling with the discipline and technical requirements of space missions. There are conflicts between the blue-collar drillers and the professional astronauts, particularly regarding their methods and attitudes. Romance develops between A.J. and Grace, causing tension with Harry, who is protective of his daughter.

**The Mission**
The team launches into space aboard two Space Shuttles and successfully lands on the moving asteroid. However, they face numerous challenges:
- Navigating the treacherous, unpredictable asteroid surface
- Equipment malfunctions and technical failures
- Life-threatening accidents during the drilling operation
- Internal conflicts and personal drama among the crew

**Climax and Sacrifice**
As conditions deteriorate and time runs out, Harry Stamper recognizes that the drilling operation will fail unless someone stays behind to manually detonate the nuclear device. In a heroic sacrifice, Harry volunteers for the suicide mission, saying goodbye to Grace and A.J. via video transmission before manually detonating the bomb, successfully destroying the asteroid while sacrificing his own life.

**Resolution**
The world is saved thanks to Harry's sacrifice, and the surviving crew members return to Earth as heroes. The film ends with Grace coping with her father's death but finding peace in knowing that he died to save humanity, while she and A.J. look toward their future together.

The movie was directed by Michael Bay and produced by Jerry Bruckheimer. It was one of two major asteroid disaster films released in 1998 (along with "Deep Impact") and became the highest-grossing film of that year worldwide, earning over $553 million at the box office.

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.




## Plot

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

*Deep Impact* was released in the same summer as the similarly themed *Armageddon*, which fared better at the box office, while astronomers described *Deep Impact* as being more scientifically accurate.[4][5] Both films were similarly received by critics, with *Armageddon* scoring 43% and *Deep Impact* scoring 45% on Rotten Tomatoes. *Deep Impact* grossed over $349.5 million worldwide on an $80 million production budget. ## Plot

[edit]

In May 1998, at a star party in Virginia, teenage amateur astronomer Leo Biederman observes an unidentified object in the night sky. He sends a picture to astronomer Dr. Marcus Wolf, who realizes it is a comet on collision course with Earth. Wolf dies in a car crash while racing to raise the alarm.

**Plot Summary (from the available information):**
The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers who are sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Bruce Willis plays Harry Stamper, the leader of the drilling team.

**Production Details:**
- Bruce Willis was cast as part of a three-picture deal to compensate the studio for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*
- Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Harry Stamper, but director Michael Bay decided on a younger actor after meeting real oil drillers
- Principal photography ran from August 27, 1997 to January 29, 1998
- An additional $3 million was added to the budget in May 1998 to include extra special effects showing an asteroid impacting Paris
- The film was released the same summer as the similarly-themed *Deep Impact*, though astronomically speaking, *Deep Impact* was considered more scientifically accurate

**Critical Reception:**
The film received mixed reviews from critics but was a commercial success. It was nominated for four Academy Awards: Best Sound, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound Editing, and Best Original Song.

In 1998, Bay again collaborated with Jerry Bruckheimer, this time as a co-producer, as well as directing the action-adventure film *Armageddon*.[31][32] The film, about a group of tough oil drillers who are sent by NASA to deflect an asteroid from a collision course with Earth, starred Bruce Willis, Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck and Liv Tyler. It was nominated for four Oscars at the 71st Academy Awards, including Best Sound, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound Editing and Best Original Song.[33] It earned $9.6 million on its opening day and $36.5 million through the first weekend.[34] Its budget of $140 million was one of the highest of the summer of 1998. It went on to gross over $553 million worldwide, the highest-grossing film of that year.[35]

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

## Basic Plot Summary of "Armageddon" (1998)

### 1. Asteroid Threat Discovery
The film begins with NASA discovering a massive asteroid the size of Texas hurtling toward Earth on a collision course that would cause global extinction. Astronomers spot it during routine observations and realize it will impact Earth in just 18 days, giving humanity an extremely short window to respond.

### 2. Recruitment of the Oil Drillers
NASA realizes their only option is to land on the asteroid and drill a deep hole to plant a nuclear device that will split it apart. However, their astronauts don't have the drilling expertise needed. NASA director Dan Truman (Billy Bob Thornton) recruits Harry Stamper (Bruce Willis), the world's best deep-core driller, and his roughneck oil drilling team from the Gulf of Mexico. Stamper initially refuses but agrees when he learns of the threat and the stakes.

### 3. Training Sequence
The blue-collar drillers are brought to NASA headquarters for intense astronaut training. Culture clashes immediately erupt between the disciplined military personnel and the wild, undisciplined drillers. The training scenes show their struggles with zero gravity, spacewalks, and spacecraft systems, while also developing relationships - particularly between A.J. Frost (Ben Affleck) and Harry's daughter Grace (Liv Tyler).

### 4. The Space Mission
The drillers launch aboard two space shuttles, Freedom and Independence, rendezvousing with a Russian space station for refueling before continuing to the asteroid. The journey includes dangerous space debris encounters and rocket malfunctions, with one shuttle (Independence) being destroyed during landing approach on the asteroid.

### 5. Events on the Asteroid
The surviving shuttle lands on the asteroid, but they face numerous challenges: rough terrain, unstable ground, equipment failures, and the asteroid's rapid rotation making drilling extremely difficult. Several crew members die during the operation, and critical equipment fails, forcing them to improvise.

### 6. Ultimate salvation
With the primary drilling plan failing and time running out, Harry Stamper makes the ultimate sacrifice. He stays behind to manually detonate the nuclear bomb while the remaining crew escapes. The asteroid successfully splits into two large pieces that safely pass Earth, saving humanity. The film ends with the surviving crew returning as heroes and memorials for those who died.

### 1. Asteroid Threat Discovery
The film begins with NASA discovering a massive asteroid the size of Texas hurtling toward Earth on a collision course that would cause global extinction. Astronomers spot it during routine observations and realize it will impact Earth in just 18 days, giving humanity an extremely short window to respond.

### 2. Recruitment of the Oil Drillers
NASA realizes their only option is to land on the asteroid and drill a deep hole to plant a nuclear device that will split it apart. However, their astronauts don't have the drilling expertise needed. NASA director Dan Truman (Billy Bob Thornton) recruits Harry Stamper (Bruce Willis), the world's best deep-core driller, and his roughneck oil drilling team from the Gulf of Mexico. Stamper initially refuses but agrees when he learns of the threat and the stakes.

### 3. Training Sequence
The blue-collar drillers are brought to NASA headquarters for intense astronaut training. Culture clashes immediately erupt between the disciplined military personnel and the wild, undisciplined drillers. The training scenes show their struggles with zero gravity, spacewalks, and spacecraft systems, while also developing relationships - particularly between A.J. Frost (Ben Affleck) and Harry's daughter Grace (Liv Tyler).

### 4. The Space Mission
The drillers launch aboard two space shuttles, Freedom and Independence, rendezvousing with a Russian space station for refueling before continuing to the asteroid. The journey includes dangerous space debris encounters and rocket malfunctions, with one shuttle (Independence) being destroyed during landing approach on the asteroid.

### 5. Events on the Asteroid
The surviving shuttle lands on the asteroid, but they face numerous challenges: rough terrain, unstable ground, equipment failures, and the asteroid's rapid rotation making drilling extremely difficult. Several crew members die during the operation, and critical equipment fails, forcing them to improvise.

### 6. Ultimate salvation
With the primary drilling plan failing and time running out, Harry Stamper makes the ultimate sacrifice. He stays behind to manually detonate the nuclear bomb while the remaining crew escapes. The asteroid successfully splits into two large pieces that safely pass Earth, saving humanity. The film ends with the surviving crew returning as heroes and memorials for those who died.

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. This additional footage, incorporated two months prior to the film's release, was specifically added for the television advertising campaign to visually differentiate the film from *Deep Impact* which was released a few months before.[13] At a budget of $140 million, it was Buena Vista's most expensive film at the time.[14]

*Deep Impact* was released in the same summer as the similarly themed *Armageddon*, which fared better at the box office, while astronomers described *Deep Impact* as being more scientifically accurate.[4][5] Both films were similarly received by critics, with *Armageddon* scoring 43% and *Deep Impact* scoring 45% on Rotten Tomatoes. *Deep Impact* grossed over $349.5 million worldwide on an $80 million production budget. It was the final film by cinematographer Dietrich Lohmann, who died before the film's release.[6]




## Plot

[edit]

In May 1998, at a star party in Virginia, teenage amateur astronomer Leo Biederman observes an unidentified object in the night sky. He sends a picture to astronomer Dr. Marcus Wolf, who realizes it is a comet on collision course with Earth. Wolf dies in a car crash while racing to raise the alarm.

The origins of *Deep Impact* started in the late 1970s when producers Richard Zanuck and David Brown approached Paramount Pictures proposing a remake of the 1951 film *When Worlds Collide*.[7] Although several screenplay drafts were completed, the producers were not completely happy with any of them and the project remained in "development hell" for many years. In the mid-1990s, they approached director Steven Spielberg, with whom they had made the 1975 blockbuster *Jaws*, to discuss their long-planned project.[7] However, Spielberg had already bought the film rights to the 1993 novel *The Hammer of God* by Arthur C. Clarke, which dealt with a similar theme of an asteroid on a collision course for Earth and humanity's attempts to prevent its own extinction. Spielberg planned to produce and direct *The Hammer of God* himself for his then-fledgling DreamWorks studio, but opted to merge the two projects with Zanuck and Brown, and they commissioned a screenplay for what would become *Deep Impact*.[7]

# Armageddon (1998) - Complete Plot Summary

## 1. The Asteroid Threat Discovery

The film begins with a prologue showing the extinction of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago, establishing the devastating impact of asteroids on Earth.

In the present day (1998), NASA discovers a massive asteroid the size of Texas hurtling toward Earth on a direct collision course. Located in the Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter, the asteroid was knocked out of its orbit and will impact Earth in just 18 days, an event that would cause total global extinction.

**Key Discovery Scene:**
- NASA's Hubble Space Telescope and various observatories detect the threat
- Dan Truman (Billy Bob Thornton), NASA's executive director, confirms the catastrophic findings
- The asteroid is officially named "Dottie"
- The impact timeline creates extreme urgency with only 18 days to act

## 2. Recruitment of the Oil Drillers

***Armageddon*** is a 1998 American science fiction disaster film produced and directed by Michael Bay, produced by Jerry Bruckheimer, and released by Touchstone Pictures. The film follows a group of blue-collar deep-core drillers sent by NASA to stop a gigantic asteroid on a collision course with Earth. It stars an ensemble cast consisting of Bruce Willis with Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck, Liv Tyler, Will Patton, Steve Buscemi, William Fichtner, Owen Wilson, Michael Clarke Duncan, Keith David and Peter Stormare.


The film was a commercial success, grossing $553 million worldwide against a $140 million budget and becoming the highest-grossing film of 1998, and the highest grossing film to be released by Touchstone Pictures. However, the film received mixed reviews from critics.

Bruce Willis was cast in the film as part of a three-picture deal he cut with the studio to compensate them for the dissolution of 1997's *Broadway Brawler*.[8][9] He received a significant pay cut for the picture as part of the deal.[10] Sean Connery was originally considered for the role of Stamper, but Bay decided a younger actor in the role after meeting oil drillers.[11]


Principal photography for *Armageddon* began in August 27, 1997 and ended on January 29, 1998.[12] In May 1998, Walt Disney Studios chairman Joe Roth expanded the film's budget by $3 million to include additional special effects scenes by Dream Quest Images showing an asteroid impacting Paris. ## Armageddon (1998) - Second Half Plot Summary

### Specific Casualties on the Asteroid

After successfully landing on the asteroid, the team begins drilling but faces numerous challenges. During the drilling operations:

- **Oscar** (Owen Wilson) is killed when a piece of drilling equipment falls on him during a rock shower
- **Rockhound** (Steve Buscemi) becomes delirious from breathing asteroid dust and must be tied to a pole, but survives
- **Chick** (Will Patton) nearly falls into a deep crevice but is saved
- **Bear** (Michael Clarke Duncan) survives multiple close calls with equipment failures

### The Nuclear Bomb Situation and Timer Malfunction

The team successfully plants the 800-foot nuclear bomb at their designated drilling depth. However, during the final drilling attempt, their drill bit breaks off 200 feet short of their target. With the countdown timer running, they realize they won't reach the required depth.

As they struggle to fix the drill, **AJ Frost** (Ben Affleck) manages to accidentally trigger the bomb's timer with only 4 minutes remaining before automatic detonation. The remote detonator is damaged during the drilling accident, leaving them unable to trigger the bomb manually from their position.

### Harry's Sacrifice

Realizing they're out of time, **Harry Stamper** (Bruce Willis) makes the ultimate sacrifice:

1. He pushes AJ aside and takes control of the damaged remote detonator
2. Harry commands AJ to return to the shuttle and tell Grace he loves her
3. A tearful AJ argues that Harry should give him life, but Harry insists he has everything to live for while AJ is young
4. Harry stays behind to manually detonate the bomb, sacrificing himself to save Earth

As the shuttle lifts off with the surviving crew, Harry says his final goodbye to his daughter Grace (Liv Tyler) via radio: "Grace, I love you."

The bomb successfully detonates, splitting the asteroid into two pieces that both pass harmlessly by Earth.

### The Romantic Subplot Resolution

The romantic tension between **AJ Frost** and **Grace Stamper** reaches its resolution:

- Just before boarding the shuttle, AJ receives a pre-recorded video message from Grace where she reveals she's pregnant with his child
- Earlier in the film, Harry had discovered the relationship and was furious about it, even trying to sabotage AJ's mission readiness
- During Harry's final moments, he gives AJ his blessing, recognizing AJ's love for Grace
- When AJ returns to Earth, he and Grace reunite emotionally in the hangar
- Grace reveals she's pregnant, and AJ excitedly accepts his role as father

The climax involves several critical moments:

1. **Final Drilling Attempt**: The team works desperately to reach depth but their equipment fails repeatedly
2. **Timer Crisis**: The 4-minute countdown creates extreme tension as they cannot trigger the bomb remotely
3. **Harry's Decision**: Harry chooses to stay behind and manually trigger the explosion
4. **Detonation**: The bomb splits the asteroid at the last possible moment
5. **Narrow Escape**: The shuttle navigates through the asteroid debris field to return safely

The film concludes with multiple emotional moments:

- **Mission Control Celebration**: NASA officials, including Colonel Sharp (William Fichtner) and Truman (Billy Bob Thornton), celebrate the successful mission
- **Reunion**: Grace runs into AJ's arms in the hangar as the surviving crew steps off the shuttle
- **Memorial Service**: The fallen crew members are honored, including Harry Stamper who receives the Congressional Medal of Honor
- **Final Scene**: AJ and Grace look toward the sky together, with their baby to come, symbolizing hope and the continuation of life
- **Harry's Legacy**: The film ends with a dedication to Harry and his crew, showing that love and sacrifice saved humanity

The surviving crew includes AJ, Chick, Rockhound, Bear, and a few others who return as heroes. Harry Stamper is memorialized as the ultimate hero who gave his life to save the world.

The film ends on an emotional yet hopeful note, emphasizing themes of love, sacrifice, and humanity's ability to come together in crisis to overcome seemingly impossible odds.

2. Harry commands AJ to return to the shuttle and tell Grace he loves her
3. A tearful AJ argues that Harry should give him life, but Harry insists he has everything to live for while AJ is young
4. Harry stays behind to manually detonate the bomb, sacrificing himself to save Earth

The bomb successfully detonates, splitting the asteroid into two pieces that both pass harmlessly by Earth.

The romantic tension between **AJ Frost** and **Grace Stamper** reaches its resolution:

The climax involves several critical moments:

1. **Final Drilling Attempt**: The team works desperately to reach depth but their equipment fails repeatedly
2. **Timer Crisis**: The 4-minute countdown creates extreme tension as they cannot trigger the bomb remotely
3. **Harry's Decision**: Harry chooses to stay behind and manually trigger the explosion
4. **Detonation**: The bomb splits the asteroid at the last possible moment
5. **Narrow Escape**: The shuttle navigates through the asteroid debris field to return safely

**The Ending Scenes:**

The film concludes with multiple emotional moments:

- **Mission Control Celebration**: NASA officials, including Truman and Colonel Sharp, celebrate the successful mission
- **Reunion**: Grace runs into AJ's arms in the hangar as the surviving crew steps off the shuttle
- **Memorial Service**: The fallen crew members are honored, including Harry Stamper who receives the Congressional Medal of Honor
- **Final Scene**: AJ and Grace look toward the sky together, with their baby to come, symbolizing hope and the continuation of life
- **Harry's Legacy**: The film ends with a dedication to Harry and his crew, showing that love and sacrifice saved humanity

The surviving crew includes AJ, Chick, Rockhound, Bear, and a few others who return as heroes. Harry Stamper is memorialized as the ultimate hero who gave his life to save the world.

The film ends on an emotional yet hopeful note, emphasizing themes of love, sacrifice, and humanity's ability to come together in crisis to overcome seemingly impossible odds.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>I Don't Want to Miss a Thing</title>
<fragment>

"**I Don't Want to Miss a Thing**" is a song by American hard rock band Aerosmith as the theme song for the 1998 science fiction disaster film *Armageddon*, in which lead singer Steven Tyler's daughter Liv starred. It is one of four songs performed by the band for the film, the other three being "What Kind of Love Are You On", "Come Together", and "Sweet Emotion". The song was nominated for an Oscar as Best Original Song at the 71st Academy Awards of 1998, but lost to "When You Believe" from *The Prince of Egypt*.[3] The power ballad[4] was written by Diane Warren, who originally envisioned it would be performed by "Celine Dion or somebody like that".[5] The song received its airplay premiere on May 12, 1998, and was officially added to radio a week later.[6]


</fragment>
<fragment>

*Birmingham Evening Mail* commented, "Songwriter Diane Warren weaves her magic again with a bombastic power ballad from the 'Armageddon' movie soundtrack. It perfectly suits Steven Tyler's sleazy vocals as the track moves towards its strings-soaked conclusion."[12] *Daily Record* called it an "epic ballad which has Steve Tyler impersonating of Bryan Adams".[13] They also noted it as an "end-of-the-night disco favourite".[14]



## Music video

[edit]

The music video was shot at the Minneapolis Armory in 1997 and features scenes from the film along with a cameo by Liv Tyler in her role as Grace Stamper.[*citation needed*] While the band plays with an orchestra backing them in a studio filled with giant banners of NASA, the banners fall in the second chorus, revealing the studio to be the launchpad of Space Shuttle Freedom from the film, while F-15 and T-38 fighter jets fly in formation overhead.



## Impact and legacy

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The song received generally positive reviews from critics. *Billboard* wrote, "If you're among the many who adore Aerosmith when it indulges in power balladry à la "Angel", then you're in for a real treat. This tune from the imminent soundtrack to *"Armageddon"* shows the enduring rock troupe happily giving in to the romance of superstar tunesmith Diane Warren's sweet tune—but with an appropriate dash of guitar-juiced melodrama. Steven Tyler's signature belting is so intensely over the top that he frequently seems to be shrieking. It's a high-voltage performance that is matched by a collision of rock-styled instrumentation and grand, faux-classical orchestration. It's a recipe that will prove irresistible to programmers at top 40 and AC formats."[11]


</fragment>

# **Armageddon (1998) - Complete Plot Summary**

## **1. The Asteroid Threat Discovery**

The film opens with a prologue showing the extinction of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago from an asteroid impact, establishing the catastrophic potential of such events. In present-day 1998, NASA astronomers discover a massive asteroid approximately the size of Texas on a direct collision course with Earth. 

- **Discovery Method**: The asteroid, knocked from its orbit in the Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter, is detected through the Hubble Space Telescope and various ground-based observatories
- **The Threat**: Asteroid "Dottie" will impact Earth in just 18 days, an event that would cause total global extinction
- **Key Officials**: **Dan Truman** (Billy Bob Thornton), NASA's executive director, confirms the devastating findings and immediately contacts the President and global leaders

## **2. Recruitment of the Oil Drillers**

Realizing their astronauts lack the specialized skills needed for deep-core drilling in zero gravity, NASA's team concludes they need the world's best oil drillers. Truman sends his team to Texas to recruit the legendary **Harry Stamper** (Bruce Willis) and his roughneck crew.

**The Recruitment Process:**
- NASA officials arrive at Harry's offshore oil rig during a drilling operation
- Harry is initially reluctant, fearing for his men's lives and concerned about leaving his daughter **Grace** (Liv Tyler)
- The recruitment argument combines patriotism (saving the world) with substantial financial incentives (approximately $1 billion total for the crew)

**Harry Stamper's Oil Rig Crew:**
- **Harry Stamper** (Bruce Willis) - Team leader, veteran master driller, protective father
- **A.J. Frost** (Ben Affleck) - Harry's most talented but rebellious worker, secretly dating Grace

Here is the comprehensive plot summary of the 1998 film "Armageddon" directed by Michael Bay, covering the complete story from beginning to end:

## **Armageddon (1998) - Complete Plot Summary**

### **1. The Asteroid Threat Discovery**

The film opens with a prologue showing the extinction of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago from an asteroid impact. In present-day 1998, NASA astronomers discover a massive asteroid approximately the size of Texas on a direct collision course with Earth. 

- **Discovery Method**: The asteroid, named "Dottie," is detected through the Hubble Space Telescope and various ground-based observatories
- **The Threat**: It will impact Earth in just 18 days, causing total global extinction
- **Key Officials**: **Dan Truman** (Billy Bob Thornton), NASA's executive director, confirms the findings and contacts global leaders

### **2. Recruitment of the Oil Drillers**

NASA realizes their astronauts lack the deep-core drilling expertise needed for zero gravity operations. Truman sends his team to Texas to recruit legendary **Harry Stamper** (Bruce Willis) and his roughneck crew.

**The Recruitment Process:**
- NASA officials arrive at Harry's offshore oil rig during a drilling operation
- Harry is initially reluctant, fearing for his men's lives and worrying about his daughter **Grace** (Liv Tyler)
- The recruitment combines patriotism (saving the world) with substantial financial incentives (approximately $1 billion total)

**Harry Stamper's Oil Rig Crew:**
- **Harry Stamper** (Bruce Willis) - Team leader and veteran master driller
- **A.J. Frost** (Ben Affleck) - Harry's talented but rebellious worker, secretly dating Grace
- **Chick Chapel** (Will Patton) - Experienced veteran crew member
- **Rockhound** (Steve Buscemi) - Geology-savvy womanizer and mechanic
- **Oscar Choice** (Owen Wilson) - Comical, pragmatic crew member
- **Bear** (Michael Clarke Duncan) - Gentle giant with immense strength
- **Max Lennert** (Ken Hudson Campbell) - Family-oriented driller with young children
- **Fred Noonan** (Clark Gregg) - Additional crew member

**Key Personal Dynamics:**
- Harry discovers A.J. and Grace's secret relationship just before the mission, creating intense father-daughter conflict

### **3. Training Sequence**

The drillers undergo an intensive 10-day astronaut training program at Johnson Space Center:

**Training Components:**
- G-force training in centrifuges
- Spacewalk simulations in neutral buoyancy tanks
- Emergency procedure training and survival skills
- Working alongside professional astronauts including **Colonel William Sharp** (William Fichtner)

**Training Conflicts:**
- Blue-collar drillers clash with disciplined astronaut culture
- Harry struggles with trusting A.J. both professionally and personally
- Several crew members consider dropping out due to the dangers and personal sacrifices

### **4. The Space Mission**

The crew launches aboard two modified space shuttles:

**Mission Overview:**
- **Freedom** (Commander Sharp) and **Independence** (with Stamper's main drilling team) constitute the mission
- They dock with a Russian space station for crucial refueling
- Complex navigation behind the Moon hides their approach from Earth observation

**Journey Challenges:**
- Dangerous fuel transfer operations at the Russian space station
- Severe meteor shower incidents during transit damage both shuttles
- The asteroid's gravitational and radiation effects present unprecedented navigation challenges

### **5. What Happens on the Asteroid**

Both shuttles successfully land on the asteroid's surface, but at tremendous cost:

**Drilling Operations:**
- The team faces extreme difficulty drilling through the asteroid's unstable, metallic composition
- Constant meteor showers and seismic tremors threaten equipment and crew safety
- Required drilling depth is 800 feet to effectively place the nuclear device

**Casualties on the Asteroid:**
- **Oscar Choice** (Owen Wilson) is killed when drilling equipment falls on him during a violent meteor shower
- **Rockhound** becomes psychologically affected by the asteroid dust and environment
- Multiple crew members suffer injuries during near-fatal accidents
- Drilling equipment repeatedly malfunctions due to the asteroid's composition

### **6. The Climax and How They Save Earth**

**The Nuclear Bomb Crisis:**
- The team successfully plants an 800-foot nuclear bomb but their drill bit breaks 200 feet short of required depth
- During attempts to fix the drill, the bomb's countdown timer is accidentally activated with only 4 minutes remaining
- The remote detonator is damaged, preventing manual triggering from their position

**Harry's Ultimate Sacrifice:**
- **Harry Stamper** decides to stay behind and manually detonate the bomb
- He pushes A.J. aside and takes control of the damaged remote detonator
- Harry orders A.J. to return to the shuttle and tell Grace he loves her
- A tearful A.J. protests, but Harry insists A.J. has everything to live for while he has lived a full life

**Final Communication:**
- Harry speaks his final words to Grace via radio: "Grace, I love you"
- The surviving crew boards the shuttle as Harry makes his final preparations
- The nuclear bomb detonates successfully, splitting the asteroid into two pieces that pass harmlessly by Earth

**Resolution and Aftermath:**
- **A.J. and Grace's Future**: When A.J. returns, Grace reveals she's pregnant with his child, continuing Harry's legacy
- **Mission Control**: NASA officials celebrate the successful mission
- **Memorial Service**: The fallen crew members, especially Harry Stamper, are honored as heroes
- **Hero's Welcome**: The surviving crew return as celebrated heroes who saved the world

### **Key Emotional Arcs:**

- **Father-Daughter Relationship**: Harry's protective love for Grace drives much of the emotional conflict
- **Love vs. Duty**: A.J. chooses between his love for Grace and his duty to the mission
- **Heroism and Sacrifice**: Ordinary blue-collar workers become humanity's saviors
- **Redemption**: Harry ultimately accepts A.J. as Grace's partner and gives them his blessing

The film concludes with a hopeful note that love, sacrifice, and humanity's ability to unite in crisis saved the world from certain destruction. Harry Stamper's sacrifice ensures Earth's future continues through A.J., Grace, and their unborn child.

Its highest grossing single day was Saturday, February 14, 1998, on which it earned $13,048,711, more than eight weeks after its North American debut.[117][118] On March 14, it surpassed *Star Wars* as the highest-grossing film ever in North America.[119] It stayed at number one for 15 consecutive weeks in North America, a record for any film.[120] By April 1998, the film's number one spot would be overtaken by *Lost in Space*, dropping into second place.[121] The film stayed in theaters in North America for almost 10 months before finally closing on Thursday, October 1, 1998, with a final domestic gross of $600,788,188,[122] equivalent to $1176.8  million in 2024[123]. Outside North America, the film made double its North American gross, generating $1,242,413,080[124] and accumulating a grand total of $1,843,201,268 worldwide from its initial theatrical run.[125]

Because of release schedules—especially in the case of films released towards the end of the year—and different release patterns across the world, many films can do business in two or more calendar years; therefore the grosses documented here are not confined to just the year of release. Grosses are not limited to original theatrical runs either, with many older films often being re-released periodically so the figures represent all the business a film has done since its original release; a film's first-run gross is included in brackets after the total if known. Because of incomplete data it cannot be known for sure how much money some films have made and when they made it, but generally the chart chronicles the films from each year that went on to earn the most. In the cases where estimates conflict both films are recorded, and in cases where a film has moved into first place because of being re-released the previous record-holder is also retained.

<document>
<title>List of highest-grossing films</title>
<fragment>
Films generate income from several revenue streams, including theatrical exhibition, home video, television broadcast rights, and merchandising. However, theatrical box-office earnings are the primary metric for trade publications in assessing the success of a film, mostly because of the availability of the data compared to sales figures for home video and broadcast rights, but also because of historical practice. Included on the list are charts of the top box-office earners (ranked by both the nominal and real value of their revenue), a chart of high-grossing films by calendar year, a timeline showing the transition of the highest-grossing film record, and a chart of the highest-grossing film franchises and series. All charts are ranked by international theatrical box-office performance where possible, excluding income derived from home video, broadcasting rights, and merchandise.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On this chart, films are ranked by the revenues from theatrical exhibition at their nominal value, along with the highest positions they attained. Six films in total have grossed in excess of $2 billion worldwide, with *Avatar* ranked in the top position. All of the films have had a theatrical run (including re-releases) in the 21st century, and films that have not played during this period do not appear on the chart because of ticket-price inflation, population size and ticket purchasing trends not being considered.

[edit]

<fragment>
* *Titanic* became the first film in history to pass $1 billion at the box office on March 1, 1998. *Titanic* held the record for the highest-grossing film of all time for 12 years until it was surpassed by *Avatar* on January 25, 2010.
* The *Jurassic Park* franchise became the sixth film franchise to gross $1 billion with the release of *The Lost World: Jurassic Park*.[3]
* Sony Pictures became the year's highest-grossing distributor in the United States and Canada, with $1.3 billion in domestic gross. It was the first time Sony Pictures topped the domestic box office, after Disney was the top-grossing domestic distributor for the previous three years.[4]

<fragment>

Because of release schedules—especially in the case of films released towards the end of the year—and different release patterns across the world, many films can do business in two or more calendar years; therefore the grosses documented here are not confined to just the year of release. Grosses are not limited to original theatrical runs either, with many older films often being re-released periodically so the figures represent all the business a film has done since its original release; a film's first-run gross is included in brackets after the total if known. Because of incomplete data it cannot be known for sure how much money some films have made and when they made it, but generally the chart chronicles the films from each year that went on to earn the most. In the cases where estimates conflict both films are recorded, and in cases where a film has moved into first place because of being re-released the previous record-holder is also retained.

Some of the older films that held the record of highest-grossing film still have respectable grosses by today's standards, but no longer compete numerically against today's top-earners in an era of much higher individual ticket prices. When those prices are adjusted for inflation, however, then *Gone with the Wind*—which was the highest-grossing film outright for twenty-five years—is still the highest-grossing film of all time. The following is a **list of the highest-grossing films in the United States and Canada**, a market known in the film industry as the "North American box office",[1][2] and where "gross" is defined in US dollars.




## Not adjusted for inflation

[edit]

This is a list of the highest-grossing films in the U.S. and Canada,[3] a market known in the film industry as the **North American box office**, or as the **domestic box office** within the U.S. itself.[1][2] The chart is ranked by lifetime gross, and for comparison, the figures adjusted for the effects of inflation are also listed, using the U.S. consumer price index;[4] a film's earnings from its initial release are also included to provide a basis for comparison between films released around the same time.



† *Background shading indicates films playing in the week commencing 14 November 2025 in theaters around the world*.




</fragment>
<fragment>
This chart ranks films by gross adjusted for ticket price inflation up to 2020 levels, based on data from Box Office Mojo, which was last updated in 2019 based on an average domestic movie ticket price of $9.01, and applying the Template:Inflation for the following years up to 2022 levels, due to the lack of updates on the original source.[7] It was compiled by multiplying the average ticket price in the current year by an estimate of the total number of admissions. Where the number of admissions is unknown, they are estimated by dividing the nominal gross by the average ticket price in the year of release to provide an estimate (taking re-releases into account).[8] Admissions better reflect the popularity of older films, since they are less susceptible to the effects of inflation.


Many of the films on this list were released prior to the availability of home video and have had multiple releases.

<fragment>
The theatrical year of 1996 achieved a $5.8 billion domestic gross milestone and saw a record twelve films earning over $100 million by the end of December, with *Independence Day* earning over $300 million. However, the film industry experienced a surplus of releases between 1995 and 1996 that resulted in several box office flops, studio bankruptcies and sales, and otherwise successful films struggling to turn in a profit. The average cost of producing and marketing film rose to $60 million, a 20% increase from the previous year, with a contributing factor being the record high-salaries for stars such as Sylvester Stallone, Tom Cruise, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Mel Gibson, Jim Carrey, Harrison Ford, Michael Douglas, Sharon Stone, Julia Roberts, and Demi Moore that became the subject of industry scrutiny following several high profile flops that were released in between 1995 and 1996.

<title>Gladiator (2000 film)</title>
<fragment>

Outside of North America, *Gladiator* is estimated to have grossed over $272.9 million internationally.[70] This gave the film a cumulative gross of over $503.2 million worldwide against a budget of $103 million.[70] It was the second highest-grossing film of 2000 behind *Mission: Impossible 2* ($546.4 million).[70]


Due to an increase in ticket prices, 2000 set a new record of $7.7 billion at the domestic box office, exceeding the previous year's $7.31 billion. However, attendance was estimated at being down 2.5% from 1999.[72][73] Industry executives blamed the decrease in attendance on the year's slate for its lack of commercial appeal, a dearth of female-driven films and sleeper hits, as well as several exhibition chains filing for bankruptcy.[74][73] Nevertheless, *Gladiator* was considered to be one of 2000's biggest blockbusters due to strong word of mouth, contributing to its long-lasting box office performance and DreamWorks' improving fortunes.[75][73][74]



## Reception

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)The logo for *Gladiator*
The theatrical year of 1999 achieved a record $7.3 billion at the domestic box office, thanks largely to the success of *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace* and *The Sixth Sense*. Industry executives did not replicate that success with the releases in 2000, however. Increasing production costs and a lack of merchandising forced studios to concentrate marketing on the appeal of popular actors such as Tom Cruise, Mel Gibson, Eddie Murphy, Jim Carrey, and Bruce Willis to help boost ticket sales and draw in potential female audiences for their slates.[53][54][55]

Cameron's films have grossed over $8 billion worldwide, making him the second-highest-grossing film director of all time. Three of Cameron's films are amongst the top four highest-grossing films of all time; *Avatar* (2009), *Avatar: The Way of Water* (2022) and *Titanic* (1997) are the highest, third-highest and fourth-highest-grossing films of all time, respectively.[1] Cameron directed the first film to gross over $1 billion, the first two films to gross over $2 billion, and is the only director to have had three films gross over $2 billion.[2][3] In 2010, *Time* named Cameron one of the 100 most influential people in the world. Cameron is also an environmentalist and runs several sustainability businesses.

In 1997, he wrote, directed, edited and produced the epic romance film *Titanic*, one of the most expensive films ever made. <title>Armageddon (1998 film)</title>
<fragment>
*Armageddon* was released on July 1, 1998 in 3,127 theaters in the United States and Canada. It ranked first at the box office ahead of *Dr. Dolittle* with an opening weekend gross of $36 million, combined with $54.2 million from its first five days.[23] Upon opening, the film had the third-highest Fourth of July opening weekend at the time, behind *Men in Black* and *Independence Day*.[24] The film was dethroned by *Lethal Weapon 4* in its second weekend, although it collected a total of $23.5 million.[25] In late July 1998, it surpassed its rival *Deep Impact* to become the highest-grossing domestic release of the year.[26] The film grossed $201.6 million in the United States and Canada and $352.1 million in other territories for a worldwide total of $553.7 million.[2] It was the highest-grossing film of 1998 worldwide and the second-highest-grossing film of that year in the United States, finishing just behind *Saving Private Ryan*.

Based on official box office data from the sources I consulted, **James Cameron's Titanic (1997)** was the highest-grossing film of 1998 at the worldwide box office with a total gross of $2.2 billion.

Here's a breakdown of the figures:

**Highest-grossing films of 1998 worldwide:**
1. **Titanic (1997)** - Directed by James Cameron: $2.2 billion
2. **Armageddon (1998)** - Directed by Michael Bay: $553.7 million  
3. **Saving Private Ryan (1998)** - Directed by Steven Spielberg: $481.8 million

It's worth noting that Titanic was actually released in 1997, but continued to dominate the box office well into 1998. If you're looking for films that were specifically released in 1998, then **Armageddon** was the highest-grossing film released that year.

The confusion is common because Titanic's theatrical run was so exceptionally long and successful that it remained the top earner throughout 1998 even though it premiered at the end of 1997.

***Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace*** is a 1999 American epic space opera film written and directed by George Lucas. It stars Liam Neeson, Ewan McGregor, Natalie Portman, Jake Lloyd, Ahmed Best, Ian McDiarmid, Anthony Daniels, Kenny Baker, Pernilla August and Frank Oz. It is the fourth film in the *Star Wars* film series, the first film of the prequel trilogy and the first chronological chapter of the "Skywalker Saga". Set 32 years before the original trilogy, (13 years before the formation of the Galactic Empire), during the era of the Galactic Republic, the plot follows Jedi Master Qui-Gon Jinn and his apprentice Obi-Wan Kenobi as they try to protect Queen Padmé Amidala of Naboo in hopes of securing a peaceful end to an interplanetary trade dispute. Joined by Anakin Skywalker—a young slave with unusually strong natural powers of the Force—they simultaneously contend with the mysterious return of the Sith. The film was produced by Lucasfilm and distributed by 20th Century Fox.

<title>Mission: Impossible 2</title>
<fragment>

When *Mission: Impossible 2* first opened, the film was ranked number one at the box office, topping out *Dinosaur*.[29] It held on to the number one spot for two weekends until it was overtaken by *Gone in 60 Seconds*.[30] Around this time, the film went on to become the highest-grossing film of the year domestically, beating *Gladiator*.[31] It would remain so until that December when it was dethroned by *How the Grinch Stole Christmas*.[32] The film eventually grossed $215,409,889 in its North American release and $330,978,216 in other territories for a total worldwide gross of $546,388,105, making this the highest-grossing film of 2000.[4] It is John Woo's highest-grossing film of all time, surpassing *Face/Off*, and was the highest-grossing film in the *Mission: Impossible* series until the release of the fourth film, *Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol*, in 2011.

*Mission: Impossible 2* was theatrically released in the United States by Paramount Pictures on May 24, 2000, and grossed $546 million worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing film of that year. Initial reaction from critics was mixed, with praise for the action sequences and Woo's direction, but criticism for the characterization, deeming the film inferior to the first film. A sequel, *Mission: Impossible III*, was released in 2006.




## Plot

[edit]

Dr. Vladimir Nekhorvich, a bio-genetics scientist, sends a message to the IMF for Dimitri (Ethan Hunt's cover name), his old friend. He warns that his employer, Biocyte Pharmaceuticals, forced him to develop a biological weapon to profit from the cure. He injects himself with the Chimera virus and carries its remedy Bellerophon in a bag. However, IMF agent Sean Ambrose, who was disguised as Dimitri, goes rogue, betrays Nekhorvich, and steals Bellerophon.
